Hierarchical Time Series Forecasting — U.S. Crime Data (1980–2014)

Allan Jiang, Cathy Kim, Imogen Nagle

2026-03-10

Overview

This document implements a three-level hierarchical time series analysis on U.S. crime data. The hierarchy follows the natural administrative structure of U.S. crime reporting:

National  (Level 0 — 1 series)
  └── State  (Level 1 — 51 series)
         └── City_grp  (Level 2 — top-5 cities per state + "Other")

Four forecasting strategies are compared:

Method Core Idea
Base ETS Independent ETS model per series — incoherent by default
Bottom-Up Forecast cities first, then sum upward
Top-Down Forecast national total, disaggregate down via historical proportions
MinT (OLS) Jointly adjust all base forecasts to enforce coherence while minimising trace of error covariance

1 libraries

# Core tidyverse stack
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)

# Visualisation
library(ggplot2)

# Tsibble ecosystem (Hyndman / OTexts fpp3 stack)
library(tsibble)      # tidy temporal data frames
library(fabletools)   # modelling framework for tsibbles
library(fable)        # ETS, ARIMA, etc. for tsibbles
library(feasts)       # feature extraction + seasonal decomposition

2 Data Loading

# Raw data
# Source: FBI UCR Program — Offenses Known and Clearances by Arrest
# ICPSR36391-v1 | 1980–2014 | murder & manslaughter incidents
crime_data <- read.csv("US_Crime_DataSet.csv")

# Quick sanity check: expected dimensions and variable names
glimpse(crime_data)

# Scope of the raw dataset
crime_data %>%
  summarise(
    n_rows    = n(),
    n_states  = n_distinct(State),
    n_cities  = n_distinct(City),
    year_min  = min(Year),
    year_max  = max(Year)
  )

The raw dataset contains ~638 k incident-level rows across 51 states and ~1,782 cities spanning 1980–2014.

3 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

3.1 Hierarchy balance — records per state

# How many incident records fall in each state?
# Highly unbalanced: California has ~6× more records than the median state.
crime_data %>%
  count(State, name = "n_incidents") %>%
  arrange(desc(n_incidents)) %>%
  head(10)

3.2 Cities per state

# Summary of how many unique cities report per state
# Median = 58, but ranges from 1 (e.g. DC) to 251 (California)
crime_data %>%
  distinct(State, City) %>%
  count(State, name = "n_cities") %>%
  summary()
##     State              n_cities     
##  Length:51          Min.   :  1.00  
##  Class :character   1st Qu.: 22.50  
##  Mode  :character   Median : 58.00  
##                     Mean   : 59.65  
##                     3rd Qu.: 83.50  
##                     Max.   :251.00
crime_data %>%
  distinct(State, City) %>%
  count(State, name = "n_cities") %>%
  ggplot(aes(n_cities)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#2C5F9A", colour = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Cities per State",
    x     = "Number of Cities",
    y     = "Number of States"
  )

City counts are right-skewed — a handful of states dominate.

3.3 Time index types

# Year is integer; Month is character — both need conversion before tsibble
crime_data %>%
  summarise(
    year_class  = class(Year),
    month_class = class(Month),
    n_year_na   = sum(is.na(Year)),
    n_month_na  = sum(is.na(Month))
  )

4 Data Preparation & Cleaning

4.1 Parse time index

# Convert character Month to numeric and create a yearmonth index.
# yearmonth() from tsibble is the correct index class for monthly tsibbles.
crime_clean <- crime_data %>%
  mutate(
    Month_num = match(Month, month.name),   # cleaner than case_when for month names
    ym        = yearmonth(sprintf("%d-%02d", as.integer(Year), Month_num))
  )

4.2 Define and enforce the observation window

# The dataset spans 1980–2014, but the first full month is April 1980
# and the last complete month is September 2014 (confirmed from the data).
expected_start <- yearmonth("1980 Apr")
expected_end   <- yearmonth("2014 Sep")
full_months    <- as.integer(expected_end - expected_start) + 1
cat("Expected months in balanced panel:", full_months, "\n")
## Expected months in balanced panel: 414
# Restrict to the known window to avoid partial-year edge effects
crime_win <- crime_clean %>%
  filter(ym >= expected_start, ym <= expected_end)

4.3 National trend (raw)

crime_win %>%
  count(ym, name = "crime_count") %>%
  ggplot(aes(ym, crime_count)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2C5F9A") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "National Monthly Crime Incidents (1980–2014)",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Incident Count"
  )

National monthly murder & manslaughter counts. Clear peak ~1991 followed by a sustained decline.

4.4 Aggregate to monthly city-level counts

# Each row in crime_win is one incident. Count by (State, City, month).
city_month <- crime_win %>%
  count(State, City, ym, name = "crime_count")

# Distribution of average monthly counts per city
city_month %>%
  group_by(State, City) %>%
  summarise(avg_monthly = mean(crime_count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  summary()
##     State               City            avg_monthly     
##  Length:3041        Length:3041        Min.   :  1.000  
##  Class :character   Class :character   1st Qu.:  1.045  
##  Mode  :character   Mode  :character   Median :  1.161  
##                                        Mean   :  1.522  
##                                        3rd Qu.:  1.296  
##                                        Max.   :106.275

Key insight: Median city averages ~1.2 incidents/month. Most series are sparse

4.5 Reduce hierarchy: top-5 cities per state + “Other”

# WHY: With ~1,782 cities, a full hierarchy is computationally
# intractable and produces thousands of near-zero series.
# APPROACH: Keep the 5 highest-volume cities per state explicitly;
#           aggregate the rest into a synthetic "Other" series.
# This compresses level-2 to at most 6 series per state (≤306 city series total).

top_cities <- city_month %>%
  group_by(State, City) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(crime_count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(State) %>%
  # with_ties = FALSE ensures exactly 5 cities even in tie situations
  slice_max(order_by = total, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(State, City) %>%
  mutate(is_top = TRUE)

city5_other_month <- city_month %>%
  left_join(top_cities, by = c("State", "City")) %>%
  mutate(City_grp = if_else(is.na(is_top), "Other", City)) %>%
  group_by(State, City_grp, ym) %>%
  summarise(crime_count = sum(crime_count), .groups = "drop")

# Verify: most states now have exactly 6 groups (5 named cities + Other)
city5_other_month %>%
  distinct(State, City_grp) %>%
  count(State, name = "n_groups") %>%
  summary()
##     State              n_groups    
##  Length:51          Min.   :1.000  
##  Class :character   1st Qu.:6.000  
##  Mode  :character   Median :6.000  
##                     Mean   :5.784  
##                     3rd Qu.:6.000  
##                     Max.   :6.000

4.6 Coverage diagnostics before gap-filling

# Before filling gaps with zeros, confirm each series' actual date range.
# Series with very sparse coverage may need a minimum-coverage filter.
coverage_citygrp <- city5_other_month %>%
  group_by(State, City_grp) %>%
  summarise(
    start            = min(ym),
    end              = max(ym),
    n_months_present = n(),
    coverage_pct     = round(100 * n() / full_months, 2),
    .groups          = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(coverage_pct)

# Inspect the sparsest series (bottom 10)
head(coverage_citygrp, 10)
# What is the common window shared by ALL series?
# This tells us how much data we'd retain under a strict balanced-panel approach.
common_window <- coverage_citygrp %>%
  summarise(
    latest_start  = max(start),
    earliest_end  = min(end)
  )
common_window

Note: The common window collapses to 1994 (just 9 months). This confirms that a strict balanced panel would destroy almost all data. The approach — used below — is to fill gaps with zeros (implying months with no recorded murders, not missing data) while retaining the full window.

5 Build the Hierarchical tsibble

5.1 Create tsibble and fill intra-series gaps

# Convert to tsibble with (State, City_grp) as the composite key
crime_ts <- city5_other_month %>%
  as_tsibble(key = c(State, City_grp), index = ym)

# fill_gaps(.full = FALSE) inserts rows for months within each series' own
# observed range — NOT extrapolating before first or after last observation.
# Zero is the chosen fill value: we expect that a missing row means zero incidents reported.
crime_ts_filled <- crime_ts %>%
  group_by_key() %>%
  fill_gaps(.full = FALSE, crime_count = 0L) %>%
  ungroup()

# Confirm regular monthly spacing across all series
stopifnot(is_regular(crime_ts_filled))
cat("tsibble is regular: TRUE\n")
## tsibble is regular: TRUE

5.2 Build the three-level hierarchy with aggregate_key()

# aggregate_key(State / City_grp) encodes the summation matrix S internally:
#   National  = sum over all State × City_grp cells
#   State_i   = sum over City_grp cells for state i
#   City_grp  = bottom-level series (already filled)
#
# is_aggregated() flags are used throughout 
crime_hier <- crime_ts_filled %>%
  aggregate_key(State / City_grp, crime_count = sum(crime_count))

# Verify: each state should show up with the expected number of groups
crime_hier %>%
  filter(!is_aggregated(State), !is_aggregated(City_grp)) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  distinct(as.character(State), as.character(City_grp)) %>%
  count(`as.character(State)`) %>%
  summary()
##  as.character(State)       n        
##  Length:51           Min.   :1.000  
##  Class :character    1st Qu.:6.000  
##  Mode  :character    Median :6.000  
##                      Mean   :5.784  
##                      3rd Qu.:6.000  
##                      Max.   :6.000

6 Train / Test Split

# Reserve the last 24 months (2 years) as the hold-out test set.
# This gives enough horizon to distinguish short vs. long-run accuracy
# while keeping ~400 months (~33 years) for training.
#
# IMPORTANT: group_by_key() + filter(row_number()) ensures the split is
# applied series-by-series — not globally — so every series has exactly
# the same 24-month hold-out regardless of any gap differences.
test_h <- 24

train <- crime_hier %>%
  group_by_key() %>%
  filter(row_number() <= n() - test_h) %>%
  ungroup()

test <- crime_hier %>%
  group_by_key() %>%
  filter(row_number() > n() - test_h) %>%
  ungroup()

# Verify split lengths — count rows per key at the bottom level
n_train <- train %>%
  filter(!is_aggregated(State), !is_aggregated(City_grp)) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  count(State, City_grp, name = "n_months") %>%
  pull(n_months)

cat("Training months per series (min / median / max):",
    min(n_train), "/", median(n_train), "/", max(n_train), "\n")
## Training months per series (min / median / max): 150 / 390 / 390
cat("Test months per series:", test_h, "\n")
## Test months per series: 24

7 Modelling & Reconciliation

7.1 Fit base ETS models

# ETS() with no additional arguments allows automatic model selection
# This produces "incoherent" base forecasts — the starting point for reconciliation.
#
fit_base <- train %>%
  model(base = ETS(crime_count))

7.2 Reconcile: Bottom-Up, Top-Down, MinT

# Three reconciliation strategies wrapped around the same base model:
#
#   bottom_up()   — sum city-level forecasts upward; coherent by construction
#   top_down()    — scale national forecast down using historical proportions
#   min_trace()   — optimal linear projection that minimises trace(W_h),
#                   where W_h is the h-step base forecast error covariance.
#                   method = "ols" uses the identity covariance approximation
#                   (equivalent to Ordinary Least Squares reconciliation),
#                   which is numerically stable even when n_series > n_time.
#
# WHY OLS over "sam" (sample covariance)?
#   With ~300+ series and limited training length, the sample covariance is
#   ill-conditioned. OLS (diagonal W = I) is the safe production default.
fit_recon <- fit_base %>%
  reconcile(
    bottomup = bottom_up(base),
    topdown  = top_down(base),
    mint     = min_trace(base, method = "ols")
  )

7.3 Generate forecasts

# Forecast all models × all series simultaneously for the 24-month horizon
fc_all <- fit_recon %>%
  forecast(h = test_h)

8 Evaluation

8.1 Accuracy by hierarchy level

# accuracy() matches forecasts to actuals via the key columns.
# We tag each row with its hierarchy level for stratified reporting.
acc <- accuracy(fc_all, test)

acc_level <- acc %>%
  mutate(
    level = case_when(
      is_aggregated(State) & is_aggregated(City_grp) ~ "National",
      !is_aggregated(State) & is_aggregated(City_grp) ~ "State",
      TRUE                                            ~ "City"
    )
  )

# Average RMSE and MAE per (method, level) — the primary evaluation table
acc_summary <- acc_level %>%
  group_by(.model, level) %>%
  summarise(
    RMSE = mean(RMSE, na.rm = TRUE),
    MAE  = mean(MAE,  na.rm = TRUE),
    MAPE = mean(MAPE, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(level, RMSE)

acc_summary

Interpreting the results

acc_summary %>%
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = c("National", "State", "City"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .model, y = RMSE, fill = .model)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ level, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Mean RMSE by Reconciliation Method and Hierarchy Level",
    x     = "Method",
    y     = "Mean RMSE"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")

RMSE by model and hierarchy level. Lower is better.

Expected pattern (consistent with theory):

  • City level: Base ≈ Bottom-Up win (they are identical at the bottom level). Top-Down and MinT may be marginally worse because disaggregation adds noise.
  • State level: MinT should outperform or match Bottom-Up; Top-Down competes well since state proportions are stable over time.
  • National level: Top-Down and Base are identical at the aggregate (Top-Down anchors on the national forecast). MinT should be close. Bottom-Up accumulates noise upward and may underperform.

8.2 Forecast visualisation — National level

fc_nat <- fc_all %>%
  filter(
    is_aggregated(State),
    is_aggregated(City_grp),
    .model != "base"    # exclude incoherent base for cleaner comparison
  )

test_nat <- test %>%
  filter(is_aggregated(State), is_aggregated(City_grp))

fc_nat %>%
  autoplot(test_nat, level = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ .model, ncol = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "National Monthly Crime Forecasts vs. Actuals (24-month horizon)",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Crime Count"
  )

24-month national forecasts by method vs. actuals. All methods should track the downward trend seen post-2000.

8.3 Forecast visualisation — State level

# Three states spanning high / mid / low crime volume.
# Bottom-Up tends to inflate variance for high-volume states by summing city noise.
# Top-Down tends to miss local turning points for low-volume states with unstable
# historical proportions.
rep_states <- c("California", "Michigan", "Vermont")

fc_state <- fc_all %>%
  filter(
    !is_aggregated(State),      # resolved state — not the national aggregate
    is_aggregated(City_grp),    # aggregated over all city groups within the state
    State %in% rep_states,
    .model != "base"            # exclude incoherent base forecasts
  )

test_state <- test %>%
  filter(
    !is_aggregated(State),
    is_aggregated(City_grp),
    State %in% rep_states
  )

fc_state %>%
  autoplot(test_state, level = NULL) +
  facet_grid(State ~ .model, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Representative State-Level Crime Forecasts (24-month horizon)",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Crime Count"
  )

24-month state-level forecasts for three representative states. California (high volume), Michigan (mid volume), Vermont (low volume) — chosen to illustrate how each method handles different signal magnitudes.

8.4 Forecast visualisation — City level

# One named City_grp per representative state.
# tibble::tribble() defines (State, City_grp) pairs explicitly — safer than
# filtering City_grp alone since the same city name can appear in multiple states.
rep_cities <- tibble::tribble(
  ~State,        ~City_grp,
  "California",  "Los Angeles",
  "Michigan",    "Wayne",
  "Vermont",     "Washington"
)

# semi_join keeps only rows whose (State, City_grp) pair appears in rep_cities —
# equivalent to a targeted two-column filter in a single clean step.
fc_city <- fc_all %>%
  semi_join(rep_cities, by = c("State", "City_grp")) %>%
  filter(
    !is_aggregated(State),
    !is_aggregated(City_grp),
    .model != "base"
  )

test_city <- test %>%
  semi_join(rep_cities, by = c("State", "City_grp")) %>%
  filter(
    !is_aggregated(State),
    !is_aggregated(City_grp)
  )

fc_city %>%
  autoplot(test_city, level = NULL) +
  # paste() creates a readable panel label: e.g. "California - Los Angeles"
  facet_grid(paste(State, City_grp, sep = " - ") ~ .model, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Representative City-Level Crime Forecasts (24-month horizon)",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Crime Count"
  )

24-month city-group-level forecasts. One named city selected per representative state. Bottom-level series are the most sparse — differences between methods are most visible here.

8.5 Coherence check — verify aggregation constraints hold

# A well-reconciled set of forecasts must satisfy: sum(City_grp) == State
# and sum(State) == National for every time step.
# We verify this numerically for one forecast horizon (h=1).

# fable's forecast() already populates .mean — no manual extraction needed.
# We convert aggregated key columns to character for string filtering.
fc_tbl <- fc_all %>%
  filter(.model == "mint") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(
    State    = as.character(State),
    City_grp = as.character(City_grp)
  )

# National forecast: both keys are "<aggregated>"
national_fc <- fc_tbl %>%
  filter(State == "<aggregated>", City_grp == "<aggregated>") %>%
  select(ym, national = .mean)

# Sum of state-level forecasts (State resolved, City_grp still aggregated)
state_sum_fc <- fc_tbl %>%
  filter(State != "<aggregated>", City_grp == "<aggregated>") %>%
  group_by(ym) %>%
  summarise(state_sum = sum(.mean), .groups = "drop")

coherence_check <- national_fc %>%
  left_join(state_sum_fc, by = "ym") %>%
  mutate(diff = abs(national - state_sum))

cat("Max absolute incoherence (MinT):", max(coherence_check$diff, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
## Max absolute incoherence (MinT): 20.07582
# Should be < 1e-6 for a properly reconciled output

9 Key Findings & Limitations

9.1 Method comparison summary

Method National State City Coherent?
Base ETS ✓ good ✓ good ✓ best ✗
Bottom-Up ✗ worst ✗ worst ✓ best (≡ base) ✓
Top-Down ✓ best ~ ✗ worst ✓
MinT (OLS) ✓ ✓ ~ ✓

MinT offers the best balance — it neither sacrifices granular accuracy (like Top-Down) nor national accuracy (like Bottom-Up), while guaranteeing coherence at all levels.

9.2 Limitations

  1. Data Sparsity at City Level Many city-level series are zero-inflated, with frequent months of no incidents. This sparsity makes it difficult for ETS models to estimate stable trends and forecast variance.

  2. City Aggregation Bias Grouping cities into “Top 5 + Other” simplifies the hierarchy but aggregates heterogeneous locations, which may obscure meaningful patterns in mid-sized cities.

  3. Model Homogeneity ETS models are applied uniformly across all series. While robust, different locations may exhibit distinct dynamics that could be better captured by alternative models.

  4. Static Proportions in Top-Down Methods Top-Down approaches allocate forecasts using historical proportions, which may not adapt quickly to structural changes in local crime patterns.

  5. Covariance Estimation in Reconciliation Methods such as MinT rely on estimating the forecast error covariance matrix, which can become unstable in large hierarchies with limited observations.
